content: Has anyone found productive use cases for the new JEV models in math formalization?

It would be interesting to continually train such a model to output true/false/undecidable probabilities for any (Lean-formalized?) mathematical statement. It would offer fast surprisal signals for an automated research system to focus on lines of investigations / proof searches with highest chance to update beliefs most significantly, and enable recursive self-improvement in mathematics.

A system-one model may not be of much help here.

According to Jev Team's The bitterest lesson: "doing the right task > data > compute > algorithms". So we need to ask ourselves, what kinds of tasks in autoformalization or math would benefit from a knee-jerk-ish "semantic if", so that we would be getting something out of it better than we feed in, and in a natural way.

We are already feeding system-two-ish LLMs high quality of Lean code and getting bulk of slops out (so, not better yet), if we are looking for a next generation technique for this task, I doubt that it would be a system-one model that makes even more local optimal decisions.

I did try something fun with Jev: model the proving process as a state machine of choosing tactics, premises etc. (as some nostalgia of techniques pre-LLM) , so Jev can play lean4game games via lean-beam.
This topic was moved here from #AI authored projects > JEV by Michael Rothgang.
It is decent for filtering retrieval, checking duplication, and other more nuts and bolts tasks. Not well suited for any task involving reasoning, yet.

I was thinking more about using code to generate a range of raw-byte lean strings and having Jev auto-classify the likelihood it would clear to kernel / solve the problem you are actually looking for to enable a smarter grind process.

I experimented with Jev shortly after it came out primarily for proof search, and got promising results. Jev is cheap and fast, but my preference would be to use an open-source alternative once a suitable one becomes available.

The general idea is fairly simple: run ordinary Lean tactics to generate possible next steps (using premises), then use the classifier to decide which resulting proof states look most promising. The tactic is called jevhammer. Both the premise selector and the collection of proof steps are configurable, and the core library doesn't depend on mathlib. There's also jevselector, where I've been experimenting with premise selection.

I used codex for the implementation of all of this. The experimentation was done with a research loop in Codex. I gave it the goal and constraints and had it propose and implement general-purpose ideas, run smaller development benchmarks, write down what helped and what didn't, and iterate.

We ran a comparison on 1,024 intermediate goals sampled from distinct declarations across 131 mathlib modules in 17 subject areas. The "stricter" CPU premise selector prepares its statistics only from imported statements available before the tested theorem, excluding the benchmark declarations. The "original" selector only excludes the benchmark declarations. Here are the results:

  • jevhammer with the stricter CPU sparse/conclusion selector solved 438/1,024 (42.8%).
  • jevhammer with the original CPU selector, rerun alongside it, solved 448/1,024 (43.8%).
  • jevhammer with LeanHammer's neural selector combined with conclusion matching solved 466/1,024 (45.5%).
  • Full LeanHammer with its neural selector solved 371/1,024 (36.2%).

One thing I find interesting is how simple the CPU selector is. It combines weighted symbol overlap with discrimination trees for matching theorem conclusions. It doesn't read proof bodies or require neural training.

Some caveats. The benchmark wasn't a robust statistical test, and I wouldn't take this as a universal ranking of the tactics. The benchmark report has the full results, sampling procedure, limitations, and reproduction instructions.
This fits with my experience. I think the main axis of improvement would be cost across the 4 tests. Did you track that?
The cost is very minimal. In total I spent ~$9 on all of these tests, and all iterations of tests that I didn't mention ($5 of which was the initial free credits I got with the account :rofl: )

What backs the neural selector? A local model? I was more poking the difference with CPU + Jev vs inviting in a model.

Spending $9 on Jev is pretty crazy to me though :rolling_on_the_floor_laughing:
Oh, the neural selector is the one that's part of leanhammer. So I didn't account for that cost.

Matthew Ballard said:

Spending $9 on Jev is pretty crazy to me though

Yeah, that's true, but I did a LOT of testing.
As I overheard elsewhere, I am planning on passing on the free $5 Jev credit to my son when I expire :wink:

I wonder if jev really beats some baselines, e.g. trying non-repeat options randomly or in the given order.

From the report and the repo, there seems to be almost no ablation experiment run? (There are two small runs of 34 goals on premise reranking which suggested no gain from jev, but no run that disables proof-state guidance by jev.)

The numbers in the results are confusing, one may get the impression that jev solved ~40% of the goals. But based on the benchmark repo, IIUC, ~80% of the solves, jev was never asked, in the rest of ~20% (89 solves), "beam discharged 51, simp_all 18, grind 6, rw 5, aesop 1 and the remaining 8".

I also can't find any evidence that isolates positive contributions from jev with existing reports and data. Am I missing something?

As I said, the benchmark isn't perfect, and you're right one should do some ablations, which I haven't had time to do yet with the current setup. In particular, this is still in the middle of the automated codex-based research loop. And in general I would never say "jev solved" anything! jev is used only as a heuristic, and existing (powerful) tactics do the actual work. I should have made that clearer in the post above.

@Utensil Song -- my apologies, I looked at some of the original notes, and I did conduct some small ablations before creating these more stable repos. I am getting codex to integrate those ablations into the benchmark now.

I ran some local experiment with the same setup against random and given-order, 2+ hour in, the partial result is:

1024 goals with jev random, no jev given order, no jev Δ (jev − given order)
solved 450 (43.9%) 424 (41.4%) N/A N/A
never asked (372) 361 (97.0%) 361 (97.0%) N/A N/A
asked (652) 89 (13.7%) 63 (9.7%) 69 (10.6%) +20
· 1 try (172) 70 (40.7%) 45 (26.2%) 51 (29.7%) +19
· 2 tries (141) 14 (9.9%) 7 (5.0%) 8 (5.7%) +6
· 3 tries (339) 5 (1.5%) 11 (3.2%) 10 (2.9%) −5

(jev number taken from repo; I ran random and the asked part for given-order)

So Jev has some contribution (+20). Analysis of the jev contributed goals suggests that if the proof needs an explicit lemma chain, jev finds them while the no-jev runs exhausted the beam's full 3×4 grid (12 nodes, its maxNodes cap).

However I suspect that no-jev harness could still close the gap, e.g. by slightly widening the beam and raising the node cap.
